verses.text: Now I Paul, myself, entreat you by the humility and gentleness of Christ; I who in your presence am lowly among you, but being absent am bold toward you.
Yes, I beg you that I may not, when present, show courage with the confidence with which I intend to be bold against some, who consider us to be walking according to the flesh.
For though we walk in the flesh, we don’t wage war according to the flesh;
for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds,
throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ;
and being in readiness to avenge all disobedience, when your obedience will be made full.

Do you look at things only as they appear in front of your face? If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ’s, let him consider this again with himself, that, even as he is Christ’s, so also we are Christ’s.
For though I should boast somewhat abundantly concerning our authority, (which the Lord gave for building you up, and not for casting you down) I will not be disappointed,
that I may not seem as if I desire to terrify you by my letters.
For, “His letters”, they say, “are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised.”
Let such a person consider this, that what we are in word by letters when we are absent, such are we also in deed when we are present.

For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.
But we will not boast beyond proper limits, but within the boundaries with which God appointed to us, which reach even to you.
For we don’t stretch ourselves too much, as though we didn’t reach to you. For we came even as far as to you with the Good News of Christ,
not boasting beyond proper limits in other men’s labors, but having hope that as your faith grows, we will be abundantly enlarged by you in our sphere of influence,
so as to preach the Good News even to the parts beyond you, not to boast in what someone else has already done.
But “he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”
For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends.

footnotes.content: Paul begins by speaking straight to his conscience—and ours. He's in a tight spot: bold in letters, gentle in person. But he anchors it all in Christ's own gentleness and humility. That's the standard. Not to prove himself, but to draw his church back to Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's begging them not to force his hand. Some were accusing the apostles of walking in the flesh, of operating by worldly power and politics. Paul sees the trap: if he bids for control by earthly means, he's already lost the battle. So he does the harder thing—pleads mercy instead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We *do* walk in flesh—Paul won't pretend otherwise. But that's not where the war is fought. I've learned in my own battles that the stronghold isn't brick or bone. It's often inside: a habit of doubt, a grudge we've nursed, a lie we've believed about ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Our weapons—prayer, the Word, patience, truth—seem fragile against what the world wields. Yet Paul says they're mighty before God. I've seen it: a quiet word in season, a faithful prayer whispered in the dark, a steady life spoken louder than any sword.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every thought captive to obedience of Christ—Paul isn't soft here. He names the war plainly: imaginations, every high thing that exalts itself against God's knowledge. That's pride. That's the voice that whispers, *You're right; the Lord is wrong.* And we're called to arrest it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul won't move until the church is ready. Once their obedience is made full—once they see clearly and answer—then he'll deal with the outright rebels. It's tender: he waits for the body to heal itself, for repentance to do its quiet work first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A sharp question: Do you judge by what's on the surface? His rivals were showy—impressive to the eye. Paul was not. But both claimed Christ. So he asks: if you're truly Christ's, reconsider. Depth matters more than polish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even if Paul boasted of his authority—which he won't, not much—he'd ground it in one thing: the Lord gave it for *building you up*. That's his whole measure. Not dominion. Construction. A pastor who checks every choice against: Does this strengthen the body or tear it down?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's careful not to seem like a bully hiding behind parchment. His letters were strong—people felt that. But he didn't want them terrified. A hard truth and a soft touch together: that's the sign of a pastor who loves the flock.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His enemies mocked him: weighty letters, weak body, despised speech. We have these words—the actual criticism. But Paul doesn't rage or deny. He lets them speak, then shows what matters: Is the content true? Does the presence match the principle? That's the court.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this mockery: the gap between words and presence, between what we perform online and who we are when the screen goes dark. Paul's answer stands: let your life in the quiet room match what you've promised on the page. As of 2026-10, that honesty is more prophetic than it was in his day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What we speak from afar, we become up close. If Paul promises in a letter what he won't live by in person, he's a fraud. So his answer is quiet: what you see written, you'll see enacted. Integrity doesn't change by zip code.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Self-commenders measuring themselves by themselves—Paul saw the trap. They made their own mirrors. They praised their own reflections. But truth isn't a mirror; it's a plumb line. And they'd never picked it up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God appoints a boundary to each laborer. Paul's field reaches as far as Corinth—that's his measure. He won't boast beyond it, won't steal another's row, won't pretend that someone else's harvest is his own. Honesty about limits is a form of humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Good News goes *beyond*—but not by Paul's grasping. As Corinth grows strong, their faith expands the work. He's willing to go further, but in the Lord's expansion, not his ambition. Patience opens doors that pride locks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A quote from Jeremiah 9:24—the only boast is in the Lord. Paul wraps his defense in Scripture itself, not his own cleverness. It's the deepest move: I'm not defending *me*; I'm pointing to *Him*.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Self-approval is hollow. The man who comforts himself with his own praise is like a child talking to his shadow. But when the Lord commends? That's the only endorsement that lasts. That's the one that makes you whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
